Free loneliness tools

20 short exercises on loneliness, 2 to 9 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • The shape of your loneliness

    Rate how often a set of loneliness experiences has been true lately: feeling unseen in a crowd, having people but not closeness, missing a particular kind of company.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Build your connection menu

    Assemble a menu of ways to make contact, sized from tiny to brave, so that on a lonely day there is something small enough to actually do.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Your social energy, honestly

    Set dials for how different kinds of social contact affect you. Not a personality label; a map of what fills and what costs.

    Dials · 4 min

  • The reaching-out ladder

    Rank ways of making contact from easiest to hardest for you. Your ladder is yours; the bottom rungs are where to start on a low day.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • The company you are missing

    Choose the kinds of company you are short of right now, then put them in order. Loneliness is usually about one specific gap, not about people in general.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • When loneliness lands in your week

    Mark the times in a typical week when loneliness is most likely to find you. It is rarely spread evenly; most people have two or three predictable hours.

    Week map · 3 min

  • Drifted, not gone

    Place people you have drifted from on a grid of how much you miss them against how easy it would be to reach out. One corner is where a message would pay off most.

    Grid · 6 min

  • What loneliness tells you

    Turn over cards that show something loneliness says in its calm, reasonable voice, and on the back a second look at whether it holds up.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • A week of contact and loneliness

    Each day, log how much real contact you had, how lonely you felt, and whether you reached out to anyone. After a few days the relationship between the three gets clearer.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • What you do with a lonely evening

    Sort the things you reach for on a lonely evening by how they leave you afterwards. Some pass the time, some make it worse, and a few actually help.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • The message you have not sent

    Write your way toward a message to someone you have drifted from: who, what has stopped you, what you would actually say, and the smallest version you could send.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • Your week in company

    Divide 100 points across the kinds of time in a typical week: alone by choice, alone by default, around people, and truly with people. The gaps between the bars are the story.

    Budget · 4 min

  • Who would you tell?

    Tick the gaps in being known that fit your life right now. Loneliness is often less about company and more about having no one who holds the details.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Alone or lonely?

    Set dials that separate solitude from loneliness. Time alone can be restful or heavy, chosen or imposed, and the difference is easy to miss from the inside.

    Dials · 4 min

  • One call, right now

    A guided reach-out you do live: pick a person, decide what you will say, settle for a minute, make the call or send the voice note, then notice what it was actually like.

    Guided exercise · 8 min

  • A time you belonged

    Remember a time you had a place among people, then take it apart to see what made it work and which of those parts you could rebuild now.

    Guided writing · 9 min

  • Become a regular somewhere

    Assemble a plan for one standing place in your week where people come to expect you. Regularity is how strangers turn into familiar faces and familiar faces into friends.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Hand on heart

    A slow breath with one hand resting on your chest, for a lonely night. The warmth and weight of your own hand does more than it sounds like it should.

    Breathing · 3 min

  • The ways you pull back

    Tick the small withdrawals you recognize from the last couple of weeks. Loneliness and pulling back feed each other, and the pulling back is the part you can actually see.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Where to look for your people

    Order places you could meet people by how well they fit you, not by how good they sound. The best place to look is the one you would actually go back to.

    Ranking · 4 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
